sources.text:
Todd Blanche narrowly confirmed as new attorney general in latest Senate vote
Washington DC - The US Senate confirmed President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche to be attorney general early on Saturday after the GOP shrugged off major Democratic concerns.
Blanche, who has already been serving as the acting attorney general since Pam Bondi was ousted in April, formerly represented Trump as his private attorney in several criminal trials before entering government.
The Senate, which Republicans narrowly control, confirmed Blanche's bid for attorney general by 50 votes to 49 early on Saturday, despite several defections among the GOP's ranks.
Republican senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski joined the Democrats in voting no, underlining the political sensitivity of the nomination.
In a post to X acknowledging the confirmation, Blanche said he was "deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice."
"I am grateful to the Senate for staying late to complete this process. To the dedicated public servants of the Department of Justice, thank you for your work each day to uphold the law and keep our country safe," Blanche wrote.
Trump, who has upended US political norms by seeking to bring nominally independent government agencies – such as the DOJ – under his increasingly direct control, calls Blanche a "star."
Democrats opposed Blanche from the beginning, accusing Trump of turning the DOJ into a political weapon.
"The attorney general is supposed to be the people's lawyer," Senator Dick Durbin, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said on Tuesday.
"Mr Blanche continues to operate as the president's personal lawyer, treating the [DOJ] like a law firm serving one client – the president."
Blanche criticized for participating in Trump's "retribution" campaign
There were doubts over whether the White House could persuade a handful of Republican holdouts, without whom even the narrow confirmation would have been impossible.
The main sticking point was an attempt to establish a $1.8 billion slush fund for what Trump calls victims of politicized prosecutions, likely including the rioters who stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.
The other main issue was an extraordinary proposal granting immunity to Trump from tax audits.
Blanche ultimately defused the internal party opposition with a written order over the weekend scrapping the so-called political "anti-weaponization fund" and saying that the audit immunity agreement with Trump would only apply "retroactively."
Since becoming acting attorney general, Blanche has been closely tied to what Democrats dub a Trump "retribution" campaign against the 80-year-old president's opponents.
Blanche has also been the target of criticism from victims of Jeffrey Epstein over the handling of the release of investigative files about the convicted sex offender, a one-time close friend of Trump.
Prior to joining the Department of Justice, Blanche represented Trump in his New York trial over alleged "hush money" paid to porn star Stormy Daniels.
He was also on the legal defense team in two federal cases brought against Trump by special counsel Jack Smith. Both cases were dropped after Trump won the 2024 election.
Cover photo: AFP/Alex Wong/Getty Images

Supporters argued Blanche’s prosecutorial experience makes him capable of managing the department and advising Trump when presidential demands cross legal boundaries.

sources.news_title: Trump’s ex-lawyer confirmed as US attorney general
sources.text:
WASHINGTON - The US Senate confirmed President Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer Todd Blanche as attorney general early Saturday after Republican lawmakers shrugged off Democratic concerns over politicisation of the Department of Justice.
Blanche, who has already been serving as the top US law enforcement officer in an acting capacity, represented Trump as his private attorney in several criminal trials before entering government.
The Senate, which Republicans narrowly control, confirmed him by 50 votes to 49. Republican senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski joined the Democrats in voting no, underlining the political sensitivity over the nomination.
Blanche said he was ”deeply honoured by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice.”
”I am grateful to the Senate for staying late to complete this process. To the dedicated public servants of the Department of Justice, thank you for your work each day to uphold the law and keep our country safe,” Blanche wrote on X.
Trump, who has upended US political norms by seeking to bring nominally independent government agencies under his increasingly direct control, calls Blanche a ”star.”
Democrats opposed Blanche from the beginning, accusing Trump of turning the Department of Justice into a political weapon.
”The attorney general is supposed to be the people’s lawyer,” Senator Dick Durbin, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said on Tuesday.
”Mr Blanche continues to operate as the president’s personal lawyer, treating the Justice Department like a law firm serving one client — the president.”
There were doubts over whether the White House could persuade a handful of Republican holdouts, without whom even the narrow confirmation would have been impossible.
The main sticking point was an attempt to establish a $1.8 billion fund for what Trump calls victims of politicised prosecutions, likely including the rioters who stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021 in an attempted insurrection to prevent Joe Biden from being certified as president, after he had defeated Trump in the 2020 election.
The other main issue was an extraordinary proposal granting immunity to Trump from tax audits.
‘Retribution’ campaign
Blanche ultimately defused the internal party opposition with a written order over the weekend scrapping the so-called political ”anti-weaponisation fund” and saying that the audit immunity agreement with Trump, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization would only apply ”retroactively” to the past tax years and not future filings.
Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since Trump fired Pam Bondi, another political loyalist, in April.
Since then, he has been closely tied to what Democrats dub a Trump ”retribution” campaign against the 80-year-old president’s opponents.
Blanche has also come in for criticism from victims of Jeffrey Epstein over the handling of the release of investigative files about the convicted sex offender, a one-time close friend of Trump.
Prior to joining the Department of Justice, Blanche represented Trump in his New York trial over alleged ”hush money” paid to porn star Stormy Daniels.
He was also on the legal defence team in two federal cases brought against Trump by special counsel Jack Smith — for allegedly mishandling classified documents after leaving the White House, and for seeking to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.
Both cases were dropped after Trump won the 2024 election.

sources.news_title: Senate Confirms Todd Blanche as Attorney General
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s nominee for attorney general, Todd Blanche, has been confirmed in a late-night vote in the Senate after a handful of fellow Republicans reconsidered their opposition.
Blanche was confirmed in a 50–49 vote in the early hours of Aug. 8, with Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) voting in opposition. The deciding vote was cast by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who announced on Friday that he believed Blanche was the best option that Trump would put forward.
“I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation’s 88th Attorney General,” Blanche said in a statement on social media, adding that he’s grateful to the Senate “for staying late to complete this process.”
The vote brought to a close weeks of tension and uncertainty over the nomination of Blanche, who has served as acting attorney general since April after previously serving as the Justice Department’s second-ranking official.
In his statement, Blanche thanked the staff at the Department of Justice, praising them for their “work each day to uphold the law and keep our country safe.”
“God bless America,” he said.
Before the deciding late-night vote was cast, the Senate worked throughout the evening on Aug. 7, with several short recesses, but procedural steps were still needed before the nomination could reach the final stage.
Earlier in the day, Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), who chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he expected a confirmation vote quickly.
He previously took several steps to address concerns raised by GOP holdouts.
Two members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, initially withheld support at a time when Blanche needed votes from all 11 Republicans on the committee. The July 11 death of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) created a vacancy on the committee and left Republicans with only a one-vote majority over Democrats.
That committee’s approval was needed to advance Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate.
Graham’s successor, his sister Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), later joined the committee and voted in his favor along with all of her GOP colleagues on Aug. 4.
“I was pleased to support President Trump’s choice for Attorney General: Todd Blanche,” she wrote on X that day, expressing confidence that he would “faithfully uphold our nation’s laws and keep law abiding Americans safe.”
She urged the Senate to move ahead with his nomination in the full Senate “as soon as possible,” rather than leaving the vote unresolved and going on an extended recess as scheduled, from the close of business on Aug. 7 and returning to session Sept. 14.
Tillis and Cornyn reversed their positions and decided to support the nominee after Blanche and the Justice Department complied with their demands.
Both senators had insisted that Blanche rescind an order that created a controversial compensation fund for people alleging they were victims of politically motivated prosecutions. Trump had advocated devoting his $1.8 billion settlement from the IRS for that purpose; the president had sued over the agency’s leaking of his personal tax returns.
Before that, at Tillis’s insistence, Blanche met with accusers of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein who criticized the Justice Department’s handling of the Epstein investigation and release of records about the case.

sources.news_title: US Senate confirms Trump's ex-lawyer Blanche as attorney general
Todd Blanche, who defended Donald Trump in criminal cases, confirmed as US attorney general
sources.text:
Todd Blanche, who risked his career as a prestigious member of New York’s legal establishment to keep Donald Trump out of jail, was confirmed on Saturday (8 August) as the attorney general.
Todd Blanche, 52, will now permanently act as the nation’s top law enforcement officer under the leadership of his former client.
He was confirmed by a vote of 50 to 49 with GOP Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski voting with Democrats against the nomination.
Confirmation was never guaranteed. Republicans Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska crossed over to vote with every Senate Democrat against Blanche. A late reversal from a third sceptical Republican, Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, pushed Blanche over the line on Friday.
Both women pointed to the same worry: that the department under Blanche has stopped acting as a check on the president. "The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration," Murkowski said. "I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case."
The clearest source of unease was a deal Blanche helped broker: a settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. Its terms gave Trump, two of his sons and his businesses immunity from tax audits, and created a $1.8 billion fund to compensate people the president says were persecuted by the government, potentially including some charged over the January 6, 2021 assault on the Capitol.
Republicans John Cornyn and Thom Tillis delayed the nomination over the fund until Blanche gave written assurance on Sunday night that it would not proceed and that the audit immunity would be narrowed. That satisfied them, but not Collins or Murkowski, who said Blanche's role in designing the deal, not just its final terms, was disqualifying.
Murkowski added the commitments "could be undone and the fund could too easily be restored" once Blanche no longer needed Senate votes, and cited the department's handling of the Epstein files and Blanche's assurances to anti-abortion groups on enforcing the reversal of Roe v. Wade.
Rather than surrender the audit immunity or formally kill the fund, which he said this week he still hopes to revive, Trump signalled he would sooner leave Blanche running the department indefinitely in an acting capacity.
That threat shaped Cassidy's decision.
Cassidy called Todd Blanche's role in the fund "poor judgment" but said private talks left him believing Blanche now saw it as a mistake, and argued confirmation would give Blanche "greater leverage to push for things that should be pushed for" than one left in limbo.
Cassidy grew emotional announcing his vote. "I'll be criticized for this vote," he said. "What's new?" He added that his constituents could be "assured that I worked hard to understand the issue and to make the right decision." Murkowski said she respected the thought he had put into it: "We both have to live with our choices, live with our votes, and trust that we have done the best job that we can."
The vote changed less than it might appear. Blanche has been acting attorney general since Bondi was fired in April, and reportedly ran the department well before that. One official called the confirmation simply: "This is exactly what he's been waiting for."
Under Todd Blanche, the department has indicted figures including former FBI director James Comey, subpoenaed records aimed at unmasking journalists' sources, stood up and then abandoned the anti-weaponization fund, and finalised the IRS immunity deal. When the Epstein files controversy sidelined Bondi from television, Blanche managed the crisis himself, a pattern expected to continue.
A career federal prosecutor turned partner at Cadwalader, Wickersham and Taft, Blanche agreed in April 2023 to represent Trump, then facing three federal indictments, surprising colleagues who knew him as an apolitical registered Democrat.
Blanche sat beside Trump through the hush-money trial, helped delay sentencing until after the election, and later helped secure a Supreme Court ruling expanding presidential immunity, plus a dismissal of the classified documents case in Florida. Nominated as deputy attorney general despite saying he wanted no government post, Blanche impressed Trump as frustration grew with Bondi, moving into her office within a week of her dismissal.

US Senate Republicans have narrowly confirmed Todd Blanche to be President Donald Trump's attorney general, capping one of the most contentious cabinet fights of Trump's second term after bipartisan concerns over Mr Blanche's independence nearly derailed the nomination.
The Republican-led Senate voted 50–49 to make Mr Blanche the second confirmed attorney general since Mr Trump returned to the White House last year with a stated desire to use the law enforcement agency to investigate his political enemies.
While Mr Blanche has already been leading the department in an acting capacity, his confirmation could free him to pursue the Trump administration's agenda even more aggressively.
The vote followed a tumultuous confirmation fight that exposed deep concerns — from some Republicans as well as Democrats — about installing Mr Trump's close ally atop a Justice Department that historically prided itself on its independence from the White House.
In the end, Mr Blanche was confirmed by the narrowest of margins, opposed by two Republicans — Senator Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.
On social media, Mr Blanche said he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me,” adding he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him.
The path to confirmation for Mr Blanche was unusually rocky, due in large part to Republican concerns about a controversial settlement of Mr Trump's lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.
Under pressure, Mr Blanche publicly promised in writing that the department would abandon Mr Trump's proposed $US 1.8 billion ($2.5 billion) compensation fund for the president's allies, including those who attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021, and rein in another piece of the settlement designed to shield Mr Trump and his family from IRS tax audits.
His appeals were enough to win over Republican Bill Cassidy, the decisive vote who threw his support behind Mr Blanche on Friday morning, local time.
Mr Cassidy said no other nominee may be able to run the department better under Mr Trump and suggested Mr Blanche's role as Mr Trump's former criminal defense lawyer could make him more effective at pushing back on the president's demands.
"This is not a referendum on President Trump," Senator Cassidy said, who lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general in a vote early Saturday morning, cementing President Donald Trump’s former personal attorney’s command of a Justice Department the Republican president has sought to bend to his will.
The Republican-led Senate voted 50-49 to make Blanche the second confirmed attorney general since Trump returned to the White House last year with a stated desire to use the law enforcement agency to investigate his political enemies. While Blanche has already been leading the department in an acting capacity, his confirmation could free him to pursue the Trump administration’s agenda even more aggressively.
Blanche said on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me,” adding that he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him.
The vote followed a tumultuous confirmation fight that exposed deep concerns — from some Republicans as well as Democrats — about installing Trump’s close ally atop a Justice Department that historically prided itself on its independence from the White House.
In the end, Blanche was confirmed by the narrowest of margins, opposed by two Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — and by every Democrat.
The path to confirmation for Blanche was unusually rocky, due in large part to Republican concerns about a controversial settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.
Under pressure, Blanche publicly promised in writing that the department would abandon Trump’s proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund for the president’s allies, including those who attacked the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, and rein in another piece of the settlement designed to shield Trump and his family from IRS tax audits.
His appeals were enough to win over Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, the decisive vote who threw his support behind Blanche Friday morning. Cassidy said no other nominee may be able to run the department better under Trump and suggested Blanche’s role as Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer can make him more effective at pushing back on the president’s demands.
“This is not a referendum on President Trump. It is a decision regarding Mr. Blanche in very specific circumstances,” said Cassidy, who lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger.
Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said confirming Blanche would be a “serious mistake.” He begged his colleagues not to be on the “wrong side” of history.
“If there is ever a moment in history when we need an Attorney General above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it’s right now,” Durbin said.
Blanche’s loyalty to Trump left senators skeptical
The vote capped off a bruising confirmation fight, with Blanche’s loyalty to Trump at the center of the stalemate.
Blanche was elevated to the top Justice Department post in an acting capacity after Trump fired Pam Bondi in April. The controversial settlement threatened to torpedo Blanche’s nomination until he formally rescinded the fund in writing under pressure from Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina. The deal reached between the senators and the department unlocked a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee, which advanced Blanche’s nomination earlier this week
Even after the deal, Blanche faced opposition from some Republican senators concerned with the “Anti-Weaponization Fund” and the tax audit immunity deal.
Murkowski announced early Friday that she would join Collins in opposing Blanche’s nomination, saying the country needs an attorney general “who will check the worst impulses of this administration.”
Former prosecutor rises as Trump’s defender
A former federal prosecutor in New York, Blanche rose to public prominence as a lead attorney on Trump’s defense team, including during the Republican’s hush money trial in New York. He also defended Trump against criminal charges in the two federal cases brought by the Biden administration’s Department of Justice — an experience Blanche has said provided him a firsthand look at what he contends was the weaponization of the criminal justice system against Trump.
Blanche entered the Justice Department last year as deputy attorney general under Bondi, overseeing the agency’s day-to-day operations and serving as the public face for high-profile and controversial matters, like the release of millions of investigative files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Democrats have accused Blanche of prioritizing his loyalty to Trump above all else through investigations against Trump foes such as former FBI Director James Comey and a radical reshaping of the department. Under Bondi and Blanche’s leadership, the department has lost thousands of employees through firings, resignations or voluntary departures.
Blanche’s supporters say his experience as a federal prosecutor and the trust he earned from Trump in the courtroom make him better equipped than Bondi to explain to the White House the legal constraints of its demands. Republicans have also touted his efforts to bring down violent crime, tackle illegal immigration and combat violent cartels and drug trafficking.
Sen. Chuck Grassley, the Republican chairman of the Judiciary Committee, gave a full-throated endorsement of Blanche ahead of voting, saying he’s led the Justice Department with distinction. “Mr. Blanche is the right choice,” he said.
But it remains unclear whether Blanche will fare any better in delivering on Trump’s desire for retribution than Bondi, whom Trump fired amid resistance from judges, grand jurors and the department’s own workforce as prosecutors sought to establish criminal conduct by one Trump foe after another.
Shortly after Blanche took the top post, the Justice Department moved to indict Comey on charges of threatening the 47th president by posting a social media photograph of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47.” Comey’s lawyers are pressing to have the case dismissed, accusing the department of misleading judges, submitting documents containing false statements and withholding key facts.
Blanche has also appointed Joseph diGenova, a former Justice Department prosecutor from the Reagan administration, to oversee a Florida-based investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired over the last decade to undermine Trump. But it remains uncertain whether that probe will result in any criminal charges.

Todd Blanche confirmed as US attorney general after tight Senate vote
The US Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general after a razor-thin vote. His elevation puts a close Trump ally atop the Justice Department despite deep concerns over its independence.
The US Senate early on Saturday confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general by a 50-49 vote, giving President Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer formal control of the Justice Department. Blanche had already been leading the department in an acting capacity after Trump fired Pam Bondi in April.
The confirmation followed a bitter fight that highlighted concerns among Democrats and some Republicans about placing a close Trump ally at the head of a department that has traditionally stressed its independence from the White House. Blanche was confirmed by the narrowest of margins, with Republican senators Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska voting against him.
Blanche’s path to confirmation was unusually difficult, largely because of Republican unease over a settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. Under pressure, Blanche promised in writing that the department would drop Trump’s proposed USD 1.8 billion compensation fund for the president’s allies, including those who attacked the Capitol on January 6, 2021. He also agreed to scale back another part of the settlement that was designed to protect Trump and his family from IRS tax audits.
That assurance helped win over Republican senator Bill Cassidy, whose support proved decisive. Cassidy said no other nominee might be better placed to run the department under Trump and suggested Blanche’s past role as Trump’s criminal defence lawyer could help him push back against the president’s demands. “This is not a referendum on President Trump. It is a decision regarding Mr. Blanche in very specific circumstances,” Cassidy said.
Democrats strongly opposed the nomination. Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said confirming Blanche would be a “serious mistake” and urged colleagues not to be on the “wrong side” of history. “If there is ever a moment in history when we need an Attorney General above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it’s right now,” Durbin said.
Blanche’s loyalty to Trump remained central to the debate. After taking charge in an acting role, he moved quickly to advance the president’s priorities, including speeding up investigations into Trump’s perceived opponents and announcing the settlement that created the USD 1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” and provided Trump and his family with immunity from tax audits. The settlement threatened to sink his nomination until he formally withdrew the fund in writing under pressure from Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis. That agreement allowed the Senate Judiciary Committee to move his nomination forward earlier this week.
Even after that, some Republicans remained unconvinced. Murkowski said on Friday that she would join Collins in opposing Blanche, saying the country needs an attorney general “who will check the worst impulses of this administration.” On the other side, Republican Judiciary Committee chairman Chuck Grassley strongly backed Blanche, saying he had led the Justice Department with distinction and adding, “Mr. Blanche is the right choice.”
A former federal prosecutor in New York, Blanche came to wider public attention as a leading lawyer on Trump’s defence team, including in the hush money case in New York. He also represented Trump in the two federal criminal cases brought by the Biden administration’s Justice Department, which Blanche has cited as proof of what he calls the weaponisation of the criminal justice system against Trump. He joined the department last year as deputy attorney general under Bondi and handled day-to-day operations, while also becoming the public face of major and controversial issues such as the release of millions of investigative files linked to Jeffrey Epstein.
Democrats have accused Blanche of putting loyalty to Trump above all else, pointing to investigations targeting Trump opponents such as former FBI director James Comey and to a broader overhaul of the department. Under Bondi and Blanche, the department has lost thousands of employees through firings, resignations and voluntary departures. Supporters say his background as a federal prosecutor and the trust he built with Trump make him better able to explain the legal limits of White House demands, and Republicans have also highlighted his work on violent crime, illegal immigration, violent cartels and drug trafficking.
It is still unclear whether Blanche will be more successful than Bondi in carrying out Trump’s push for retribution. Soon after Blanche took over, the Justice Department moved to indict Comey over a social media photograph of seashells arranged as “86 47”, saying it amounted to a threat against the 47th president. Comey’s lawyers are seeking to have the case dismissed, accusing the department of misleading judges, filing documents with false statements and withholding important facts. Blanche has also appointed Joseph diGenova, a former Justice Department prosecutor from the Reagan administration, to oversee a Florida-based investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired over the past decade to undermine Trump, though it remains unclear whether that inquiry will lead to criminal charges. The Senate vote now leaves Blanche confirmed as attorney general after a bruising contest that turned on his closeness to Trump and on questions over how far the Justice Department may be used to serve the president’s agenda.

Blanche won confirmation in a 50-49 vote, with Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska opposing him. Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana was the deciding vote after announcing Friday he thought Blanche was the best option Trump would put forward.

Republican senators had raised concerns about Blanche’s handling of the release of Jeffrey Epstein-related documents, as well as his role in establishing Trump’s $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and a related tax-immunity agreement for Trump and his sons.
But Blanche overcame those challenges in frantic meetings around Capitol Hill over the last several weeks, ultimately agreeing in writing to narrow the tax-immunity agreement and end the “weaponization” payments, which critics have called a slush fund for Trump’s allies, including those who rioted at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
Both the tax-immunity agreement, which barred the IRS from auditing previous tax returns of Trump, his sons and their family business, and the fund emerged from Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service.

Questions remain, though, about whether that commitment is legally binding, and whether Trump, who has said he loves the idea of the fund, could later press Blanche, his former personal attorney, to revive a similar program under another name.
That concern was central to the last two Republican senators Blanche needed to convince — Bill Cassidy and Lisa Murkowski — both of whom met with Blanche on Wednesday after signaling they had not yet decided how they would vote. Murkowski had cited her lack of confidence in Blanche to “check the worst impulses of this administration.”
“I take issue with the handling of the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators,” Murkowski said in a post on social media platform X.
Cassidy, who represents Louisiana, criticized Blanche’s role in settling Trump’s IRS lawsuit but said he ultimately trusted Blanche to give the president candid legal advice. Blanche will take the helm of a Justice Department that has undergone significant change in the first year and a half of Trump’s second term.
Under Blanche’s leadership, the department has sought prosecutions of Trump’s perceived enemies, caused the mass departures of career prosecutors, and stated that it served at the direction of the president, a break with longstanding norms of independence.
Federal judges have on multiple occasions criticized prosecutors for bringing what they described as weak cases, and grand juries have declined to indict in some instances. Political appointees also removed senior career officials seen as resistant to the administration’s agenda, significantly reducing staff in the civil rights division, the ethics office and other divisions.
Blanche has argued that he has helped bring crime to record lows and righted what he says are wrongs brought by the Biden administration against Trump and his conservative allies. Blanche’s supporters say he is committed to the Justice Department’s core mission of keeping the country safe.
“Mr. Blanche is a tough, fair prosecutor dedicated to the rule of law, and his leadership instills that same zeal throughout the entire Justice Department,” Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, the chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee who shepherded Blanche’s nomination, said on Friday.
Some Republican skeptics have said Blanche, who spent nearly a decade as a career prosecutor in New York, is likely the most palatable nominee Trump could have put forward, and that in a permanent capacity, he is more likely to resist White House pressure.

sources.text:
Senate confirms Todd Blanche as Trump’s attorney general in 50-49 vote
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was narrowly confirmed by the Senate on Saturday to lead the Justice Department on a permanent basis under President Trump.
Blanche’s nomination was approved in a 50-49 vote, with two Republicans, Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), voting with all Democrats against his confirmation.
“Mr. Blanche is nominated to one of the most important offices in our country, and he has shown that he’s up to that task,” Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said ahead of the vote. “His impressive background and the presentation at our hearing in the Judiciary Committee are proof that he’s led the Justice Department with distinction and is well suited to continue doing that.”
Grassley added, “Between his proven track record, his presentations to our committee and the support he’s received from across the country, I am convinced Mr. Blanche is the right choice to lead the Justice Department.”
“A vote for Todd Blanche is a vote for the safety of the American people.”
Blanche’s path to confirmation was precarious, with his nomination repeatedly appearing in doubt.
Senators from both sides of the aisle expressed concerns over his handling of the release of documents related to notorious sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein and a May 19 DOJ order that authorized the creation of $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and granted Trump, his family and business entities immunity from IRS audits as part of the settlement of a lawsuit the president filed against the tax-collecting agency.
Blanche, who was serving as acting attorney general when the order was signed, had declared the fund “dead” during his July 15 hearing in the Senate Judiciary Committee, but his confirmation vote was delayed after Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-NC) demanded a “written document” affirming that and clarifying whether the president and his family were shielded from future IRS audits.
Blanche’s nomination cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee earlier this week in a 12-10 vote along party lines.
With Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) absent due to ongoing health issues, Blanche could only afford to lose two GOP votes in the full Senate.
Ahead of the final confirmation vote, Murkowski and Collins announced they would not support Blanche, citing his handling of the Epstein files, the Trump-IRS settlement and what they described as an increasingly politicized DOJ that has repeatedly gone after the president’s political enemies.
That left Sen. Bill Cassidy’s vote as make-or-break for Blanche’s nomination.
Cassidy (R-La.), who voted to convict Trump of incitement of insurrection following the Jan. 6, 2021, lost his primary race in May after Trump endorsed his opponent.
The Louisiana Republican faulted Blanche for having “showed poor judgment in approving the anti-weaponization slush fund and exempting the president from IRS audits,” as well as allowing the DOJ to target the president’s political enemies, but ultimately concluded: “I will vote for Mr. Blanche.”
Blanche – a 51-year-old Colorado native and Trump’s former personal lawyer – has been the acting head of the Justice Department since April 2, when the president elevated him from his deputy attorney general post after firing Pam Bondi.

sources.news_title: Senate confirms Todd Blanche, Trump's former defense lawyer, as attorney general
sources.text:
Senate confirms Todd Blanche, Trump's former defense lawyer, as attorney general
Washington — The Senate early on Saturday confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general, installing President Trump's former defense lawyer as the nation's top law enforcement official.
Blanche narrowly won approval from the upper chamber in a 50-49 vote. Two Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — joined with all Democrats in voting against his nomination to helm the Justice Department.
Blanche's path for confirmation cleared earlier Friday when Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, announced he would back his nomination. With Collins' and Murkowski's opposition, and GOP Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky absent, Cassidy's vote was decisive.
In a social media post shortly after the vote, Blanche thanked the Senate for the early-hours vote and said he was "deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice."
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt called Blanche's confirmation "a huge win for President Trump and our country" in a statement to CBS News, adding that he will be a "phenomenal" attorney general.
"The American people will be well served by his unwavering commitment to law and order," Leavitt said.
Vice President JD Vance also cheered Blanche's confirmation, congratulating him on X and saying he will continue to aid the administration's efforts to root out fraud.
Blanche joined the second Trump administration as deputy attorney general and was tapped for acting attorney general following the removal of Pam Bondi from the role in April. Mr. Trump announced in June that he had selected Blanche to permanently lead the Justice Department.
But Blanche faced headwinds during his confirmation, as Democrats and some Republicans took issue with the Justice Department's creation of a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund to provide payouts to people who alleged they were wronged by the federal government. The program was part of a settlement agreement the department reached with Mr. Trump in May to resolve a $10 billion civil lawsuit he filed against the Internal Revenue Service over the leak of his tax returns by a former government contractor.
Senators also pushed back on a second provision of the settlement, which provided broad immunity to Mr. Trump, members of his family and his businesses from tax audits and investigations.
During his confirmation hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, Blanche told senators that the "anti-weaponization" fund is "dead," and reiterated that the department was "not moving forward" with the program amid fierce pushback from lawmakers on the heels of its creation.
But he still faced skepticism from two key Republicans on the panel, Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina.
Following weeks of negotiations with the Justice Department, though, the two senators reached an agreement with the Justice Department that clinched their support for Blanche's nomination. As part of the deal, Blanche issued an order late Sunday rescinding his initial May directive that established the "anti-weaponization" fund. He also clarified that the immunity deal applies to claims arising from already-filed tax returns and covers only the president, his two oldest sons and the Trump Organization.
With the backing of Cornyn and Tillis, Blanche advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in a party-line vote Tuesday. He needed a simple majority of votes from the full Senate to be confirmed as attorney general. But with the absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, Blanche could only afford to lose support from two Republicans and still win approval from the upper chamber.
Days before the vote on the Senate floor, Collins announced she would oppose Blanche's nomination because of "several actions that have further eroded the Department's independence," including the tax immunity deal and the "anti-weaponization" fund. Murkowski then said Friday she would vote against Blanche.
But he secured support from two other key Republicans, Cassidy and Sen. John Curtis of Utah.
Before joining the second Trump administration, Blanche represented Mr. Trump in his criminal case in New York state court that stemmed from a $130,000 "hush money" payment his lawyer made to an adult film star before the 2016 election. The president was convicted of 34 counts of falsification of business records.
Blanche was also on the legal team defending Mr. Trump in two federal cases brought by former special counsel Jack Smith: one relating to his alleged efforts to subvert the transfer of presidential power after the 2020 election and a second arising out of his handling of sensitive government documents after his first term. Both cases ended when Mr. Trump was elected for a second term.
In his role as deputy attorney general, Blanche oversaw the Justice Department's release of more than 2 million files from its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and met with Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein's longtime associate who was convicted of sex-trafficking crimes, last year. After their meeting, Maxwell was transferred from a low-security correctional facility in Florida to a minimum-security prison camp in Texas.
The Justice Department came under fire for its handling of the Epstein files when records were released that included unredacted names and personal information of survivors of Epstein's sex-trafficking operation.
Blanche acknowledged during his confirmation hearing that "mistakes were made" with some of the documents made public. He also met with survivors of Epstein's crimes at the Justice Department last month after Tillis said he would withhold support until Blanche did so.
But some of the survivors criticized Blanche for his behavior during the meeting, with one describing it as a "check-the-box exercise" designed to secure votes for his confirmation. They urged senators to reject his nomination.

sources.news_title: Senate confirms Todd Blanche as attorney general after bruising fight
Senate narrowly approves Todd Blanche as AG, capping tough confirmation fight
Blanche set to lead a Justice Department shaped to serve Trump
sources.text:
Todd Blanche, who risked his career as a prestigious member of New York’s legal establishment to keep Donald Trump out of jail, was confirmed on Saturday as the attorney general.
Blanche, 52, will now permanently act as the nation’s top law enforcement officer under the leadership of his former client.
He was confirmed by a vote of 50 to 49 with GOP Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski voting with Democrats against the nomination.
Since Trump re-entered the Oval Office, Blanche has been instrumental in reshaping the department in the president’s image, effectively switching from being the face of Trump’s defense to the face of his far-reaching retribution campaign.
He put forth legal arguments that expand the powers and protection around the presidency, oversaw the mass firings of experienced prosecutors and longtime officials, and spearheaded a legal strategy that has made judges across the nation question the department’s decisions.
And in just the few months since he was appointed acting attorney general, the Justice Department has brought indictments against political figures, including former FBI Director James Comey, issued subpoenas seeking to identify journalists’ sources, created — then abandoned — the controversial anti-weaponization fund, and approved a tax immunity deal between the president and the Internal Revenue Service.
But Blanche has been running the day-to-day operations of the department for far longer than that, and his nomination formalized what had already been the case internally for a while. CNN previously reported that even as deputy attorney general, Blanche often led meetings, including those that the attorney general was supposed to oversee.
That central role became especially consequential in one of the administration’s most volatile sagas, the Epstein files aftermath.
At one point, former Attorney General Pam Bondi was sent into a weekslong media lockdown for repeatedly bungling her television appearances discussing the Epstein matter. Blanche took her place, and, according to Bondi, continued to manage the crisis by himself.
Sources have told CNN that Blanche will have a similar strategy once officially confirmed — bringing cases that highlight what the president claims were instances of Justice Department “weaponization” against him, his allies and supporters.
He will also push forward other administration priorities, like hardline immigration cases and a crackdown on fraud involving government programs.
Managing the unmanageable
Blanche worked for years as a federal prosecutor before entering private practice about a decade ago. When he took Trump on as client in 2023, he stepped down from the white-shoe New York law firm, Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft, where he was a partner.
Trump was facing several criminal cases at the time.
Blanche’s decision in April of that year to join Trump’s legal team surprised those around him, according to multiple people familiar. He was registered to vote as a Democrat and those who know him say he did not wear his politics on his sleeve. Known as a hard-working lawyer who loved being a prosecutor, some of his former colleagues were surprised to see him take on the role and echo the rhetoric of his client. As recently as this week, some former colleagues were still baffled and trying to analyze Blanche’s transformation.
But the gamble paid off handsomely.
Quickly, Blanche became Trump’s go-to attorney to navigate three federal indictments.
Blanche was one of a select few who sat beside and advised Trump during his hush-money criminal trial in New York, when the president’s freedom was at stake. He weaved Trump’s gripes into legal briefs and adopted his arguments before the judge, drawing rebukes at times.
Although Trump was convicted, Blanche’s legal tactics helped delay Trump’s sentencing until after the election — effectively ensuring he would not serve prison time.
In a federal case accusing Trump of election interference, the Trump defense team won at the Supreme Court to expand protections from criminal prosecution for the president just before Trump won his second term. Blanche and his team also convinced a Trump-appointed judge in Florida to throw out charges in a second federal case accusing him of mishandling classified documents.
As rumors swirled that his work for Trump could land Blanche a job in the administration, Blanche told allies that he was not interested in a government job, sources told CNN at the time.
Still, he was nominated by Trump to serve as the Justice Department’s number two. At the time, Trump wrote on social media that Blanche will fix “what has been a broken System of Justice for far too long.”
Once in the job, sources say that Blanche immediately eyed the attorney general spot. His work pleased the president, sources told CNN, particularly as he became increasingly frustrated with Blanche’s predecessor, Bondi. When she was fired, Blanche seamlessly slipped into the job, even moving into Bondi’s old office the first week she was gone.
“This is exactly what he’s been waiting for,” one department official said of his confirmation.
Confirmation negotiations
Blanche’s path to confirmation was far from smooth. He spent weeks trying to get into the good graces of senators whose votes were crucial to his success, but some of his efforts were futile.
His struggle to align Republican lawmakers was most obvious with Sen. Lisa Murkowski. Despite a two-day trip to her home state of Alaska, reaching two settlements and dropping two lawsuits, and awarding more than $6 million in grants, Murkowski voted to oppose Blanche.
“The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration,” Murkowski said of her decision. “I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case.”
Blanche also concentrated on Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, who raised concerns about the “weaponization of the Justice Department,” including a probe into Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House aide and key witness in the congressional investigation of the January 6 Capitol attack.
It is unclear whether the Justice Department will move for an indictment of the ex-aide.
Blanche’s initial vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee was even delayed as he underwent tense talks with Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, both of whom had concerns about the anti-weaponization fund and the IRS deal.
In the end, Blanche signed one memo that ended the anti-weaponization fund, and released a second, unsigned memo clarifying the terms of the tax-immunity agreement.
CNN’s Morgan Rimmer and Kara Scannell contributed to this report

sources.news_title: Senate confirms Todd Blanche as attorney general after weeks of uncertainty
sources.text:
The Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as U.S. attorney general early Saturday in a mostly party-line vote, capping off weeks of uncertainty and despite bipartisan concerns about his ability to run a Justice Department independent of President Donald Trump’s impulses.
Blanche, who was formerly Trump’s personal attorney, was confirmed by a vote of 50-49, with only two Republican senators, Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, voting against him along with all Democrats.
The vote was held after 4 a.m. on Saturday, as a late-night session ran over into the early hours ahead of a planned Senate recess.
“I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation’s 88th Attorney General,” Blanche said in a post on X, adding: “I am grateful to the Senate for staying late to complete this process.”
His confirmation had been in jeopardy, largely over concerns about his handling of the so-called anti-weaponization fund, which was established in connection with a purported settlement between private citizen Trump and the federal government he now controls. That fund could have been used to give money to Trump allies who claimed they were victims of government overreach, including people who were charged in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack. Blanche had also signed off on another part of the deal that gave Trump, his family members and his businesses immunity from tax audits.
Earlier Republican holdouts, Sens. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, ultimately backed Blanche after receiving various assurances from the nominee, including an order rescinding the $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund. (A legal loophole could still revive the fund, however.)
Lawmakers from both parties had also expressed discomfort about Blanche’s personal history with the president.
“The problem with confirming Todd Blanche is that he has never been able to shed his role as criminal defense lawyer for Donald Trump. He just can’t do it,” Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., said ahead of the Senate Judiciary Committee’s vote advancing Blanche’s nomination. “He will never do what’s best for the American people. He will only do what’s best for Donald Trump, and you cannot leave someone like that as the nation’s No. 1 law enforcement official.”
Blanche took over as acting attorney general in April after Trump forced out his predecessor, Pam Bondi. Trump had become frustrated with Bondi over the lack of action from the DOJ against his political foes.
Blanche told NBC News in April, after he took over the Justice Department in an acting capacity, that Americans should be “happy” with Trump’s involvement in the Justice Department’s operations.
Weeks after Bondi’s dismissal, the Justice Department indicted former FBI Director James Comey, who is accused of threatening the president’s life by posting a photo of seashells in the shape of “8647” to Instagram.
Critics have questioned whether Blanche will stand up to Trump’s future desires to target his political enemies.
“The biggest concern is whether he is now going to be emboldened to go even more gung-ho on Trump’s campaign of using the Justice Department for retribution,” former federal prosecutor Laurie Levenson told NBC News in an interview prior to his confirmation. “There are no guardrails.”
Trump’s attorneys general in his first term also departed under pressure to act on the president’s behalf. Jeff Sessions was forced out after the 2018 midterms in part due Trump’s frustration with his recusal from the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, an investigation that led to the Mueller report. Former Attorney General William Barr left after Trump tried to enlist the Justice Department in his efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss, a campaign that culminated in the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.

sources.news_title: Todd Blanche is narrowly confirmed as Trump's attorney general in an overnight Senate vote
sources.text:
Todd Blanche is narrowly confirmed as Trump’s attorney general in an overnight Senate vote
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general in a vote early Saturday, cementing the command of President Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer at a Department of Justice that Trump has sought to bend to his will.
The Republican-led Senate voted 50-49 to make Blanche the second confirmed attorney general since Trump returned to the White House last year with a stated desire to use the law enforcement agency to investigate his political enemies. While Blanche has already been leading the department in an acting capacity, his confirmation could free him to pursue the administration’s agenda even more aggressively.
Blanche said on social media that he was “deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me,” adding that he was “grateful” to senators for working late to confirm him.
The vote followed a tumultuous confirmation fight that exposed deep concerns — from some Republicans as well as Democrats — about installing Trump’s close ally atop a Justice Department that historically prided itself on its independence from the White House.
In the end, Blanche was confirmed by the narrowest of margins, opposed by two Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — and by every Democrat.
The path to confirmation for Blanche was unusually rocky, due in large part to Republican concerns about a controversial settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS.
Under pressure, Blanche publicly promised in writing that the department would abandon Trump’s proposed $1.8 billion compensation fund for the president’s allies, including those who attacked the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, and rein in another piece of the settlement designed to shield Trump and his family from IRS tax audits.
His appeals were enough to win over Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, the decisive vote who threw his support behind Blanche on Friday morning. Cassidy said no other nominee may be able to run the department better under Trump and suggested Blanche’s role as Trump’s former criminal defense lawyer can make him more effective at pushing back on the Republican president’s demands.
“This is not a referendum on President Trump. It is a decision regarding Mr. Blanche in very specific circumstances,” said Cassidy, who lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger.
Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said confirming Blanche would be a “serious mistake.” He begged his colleagues not to be on the “wrong side” of history.
“If there is ever a moment in history when we need an Attorney General above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it’s right now,” Durbin said.
Blanche’s loyalty to Trump left senators skeptical
The vote capped off a bruising confirmation fight, with Blanche’s loyalty to Trump at the center of the stalemate.
Blanche was elevated to the top Justice Department post in an acting capacity after Trump fired Pam Bondi in April. Blanche moved swiftly to advance the president’s interests, accelerating investigations into Trump’s perceived foes and announcing the settlement that created the $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” to compensate people who feel mistreated by the criminal justice system and provided Trump and family members with immunity from tax audits.
The controversial settlement threatened to torpedo Blanche’s nomination until he formally rescinded the fund in writing under pressure from Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina. The deal reached between the senators and the department unlocked a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee, which advanced Blanche’s nomination earlier this week
Even after the deal, Blanche faced opposition from some Republican senators concerned with the settlement fund and the tax audit immunity.
Murkowski announced early Friday that she would join Collins in opposing Blanche’s nomination, saying the country needs an attorney general “who will check the worst impulses of this administration.”
Former prosecutor rises as Trump’s defender
A former federal prosecutor in New York, Blanche rose to public prominence as a lead attorney on Trump’s defense team, including during the Republican’s hush money trial in New York. He also defended Trump against criminal charges in the two federal cases brought by the Biden administration’s Department of Justice — an experience Blanche has said provided him a firsthand look at what he contends was the weaponization of the criminal justice system against Trump.
Blanche entered the Justice Department last year as deputy attorney general under Bondi, overseeing the agency’s day-to-day operations and serving as the public face for high-profile and controversial matters, like the release of millions of investigative files related to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Democrats have accused Blanche of prioritizing his loyalty to Trump above all else through investigations against Trump foes such as former FBI Director James Comey and a radical reshaping of the department. Under Bondi and Blanche’s leadership, the department has lost thousands of employees through firings, resignations or voluntary departures.
Blanche’s supporters say his experience as a federal prosecutor and the trust he earned from Trump in the courtroom make him better equipped than Bondi to explain to the White House the legal constraints of its demands. Republicans have also touted his efforts to bring down violent crime, tackle illegal immigration and combat violent cartels and drug trafficking.
Sen. Chuck Grassley, the Judiciary Committee chairman, gave a full-throated endorsement of Blanche ahead of voting, saying he’s led the Justice Department with distinction. “Mr. Blanche is the right choice,” said Grassley, R-Iowa.
It is unclear whether Blanche will fare any better in delivering on Trump’s desire for retribution than Bondi, whom Trump fired amid resistance from judges, grand jurors and the department’s own workforce as prosecutors sought to establish criminal conduct by one Trump foe after another.
Shortly after Blanche took the top post, the Justice Department moved to indict Comey on charges of threatening the 47th president by posting a social media photograph of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47.” Comey’s lawyers are pressing to have the case dismissed, accusing the department of misleading judges, submitting documents containing false statements and withholding key facts.
Blanche has also appointed Joseph diGenova, a former Justice Department prosecutor from the Reagan administration, to oversee a Florida-based investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired over the last decade to undermine Trump. But it remains uncertain whether that probe will result in any criminal charges.
__
Associated Press writers Bill Barrow in Atlanta and Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

The Senate on Saturday confirmed acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to serve as the nation’s top law enforcement official in a narrow 50-49 vote, ending weeks of Republican holdouts and intense negotiations over Department of Justice policies.
Every Senate Democrat opposed the nomination, alongside two Republicans: Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina withheld support over a $1.8 billion anti-weaponization package. Cornyn and Tillis demanded that the Department of Justice provide written documentation proving the fund had been rescinded.
They also required the rewriting of language in an Internal Revenue Service settlement to ensure audit immunity for President Donald Trump and his family did not extend beyond the named plaintiffs.
Although the Justice Department submitted a proposal to Cornyn on July 27, Cornyn initially rejected it, stating his conditions had not been met. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley postponed a scheduled July 30 markup while negotiations continued. The panel ultimately advanced Blanche’s nomination in a 12-10 vote on Tuesday after Blanche released the requested documentation confirming the fund’s termination.
Tillis had also conditioned his vote on Blanche meeting with alleged victims of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Blanche met with several accusers at Justice Department headquarters in July to satisfy the requirement, though some participants later described the meeting as dismissive and unproductive.
Separately, Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana remained undecided until announcing his support on the Senate floor Friday. Cassidy had met privately with Blanche on Wednesday after expressing concerns in a SiriusXM interview that Blanche might act as “Trump’s personal attorney who is now the attorney general.”
With Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona absent due to a family emergency, Blanche could afford to lose no more than two Republican votes to secure confirmation without former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell present.
Collins and Murkowski both cited concerns regarding the department’s independence in explaining their opposition. Both senators had previously voted to confirm former Attorney General Merrick Garland.
“While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political,” Collins said in a Tuesday statement. “Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation … More than 1,200 former Department of Justice employees have opposed his nomination, arguing that he has undermined the institution. For these reasons, I will vote against this nomination.”
Collins specifically pointed to the $1.8 billion fund, attempted indictments of Democratic Sens. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and Blanche’s commitment to prohibit the mailing of abortion pills.
Murkowski echoed similar criticisms on Thursday regarding the department’s direction.
“The politicization—even weaponization—of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it,” Murkowski said. “I take issue with the handling of the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators.”
Blanche had been serving as acting attorney general since April 2, following President Trump’s dismissal of former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

sources.news_title: U.S. Senate confirms Todd Blanche as attorney general
sources.text:
(The Center Square) — The U.S. Senate, in a 50-49 vote early Saturday morning, confirmed Todd Blanche to serve as the nation's 88th attorney general.
Blanche, who was nominated to the post by President Donald Trump after he removed Pam Bondi, faced intense scrutiny over his tenure at the Justice Department.
Blanche was first confirmed as deputy attorney general in 2025. He began serving as acting attorney general in April.
Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, voted against Blanche’s nomination. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., did not vote. Murkowski said she took issue with the Department of Justice’s nearly $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund, which was announced in May.
The fund, born out of a settlement between Trump and the IRS over his leaked tax returns, was meant to support victims of political persecution. Trump floated allowing individuals who assaulted police officers in the Jan. 6, 2021, attacks on the U.S. Capitol to receive assistance from the fund.
Blanche issued an order rescinding further operation of the fund. However, Murkowski said she does not believe the order is legally binding.
“The Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage. Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds,” Murkowski wrote on social media.
Collins took issue with the anti-weaponization fund as well. Additionally, she said Blanche has allowed the department to become “increasingly political.”
Collins pointed to the department’s attempted indictments of Sens. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., over a video where they encouraged military members to resist unlawful orders.
“More than 1,200 former Department of Justice employees have opposed his nomination, arguing that he has undermined the institution,” Collins wrote on social media.
Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., cast a critical vote in confirming Blanche, given the objections of Murkowski and Collins. He said he was concerned about the anti-weaponization fund that said it would be better to have Blanche as a Senate-confirmed nominee in order to have greater leverage over his actions.
“Mr. Blanche is not perfect and he will tell you this,” Cassidy said on the Senate floor. “The choice is not between perfection and Mr. Blanche. This is not a referendum on President Trump, it is a decision regarding Mr. Blanche and very specific circumstances.”
Cassidy pointed to Blanche’s pursuit of fraud in federal programs, as he has led the Justice Department. He applauded Blanche’s pursuit, a sentiment echoed by other Republicans.
Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, said he supported Blanche’s nomination because of the work under his leadership to reduce crime through increased prosecutions. He said the United States has experienced its lowest murder rate since 1900, in part due to Blanche's leadership of the Justice Department.
“Mr. Blanche refocused the Justice Department on keeping Americans safe,” Grassley said. “That's the sort of impact we should want and should expect from the Justice Department and any attorney general that heads that department. And that is what Mr. Blanche has delivered.”
With Blanche’s confirmation, he will need to be sworn in as attorney general in a ceremony that will likely occur in the next week.

sources.text:
Todd Blanche confirmed as attorney general
Todd Blanche, President Donald Trump’s former personal attorney, has been confirmed as the next U.S. attorney general.
Blanche, who’s been serving as acting attorney general since taking over from Pam Bondi in April, was confirmed in a narrow 50-49 Senate vote.
Todd Blanche confirmed
Big picture view:
With all Democrats opposing Blanche, his confirmation came down to a single vote in the Senate, after Republican Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski said they’d vote against his nomination.
Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a frequent Trump critic, announced Friday that he’d support Blanche, securing the necessary votes to be confirmed.
Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on August 05, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Two other Republican senators – John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina – also threatened to block the nomination, but they ended up backing Blanche after the Justice Department confirmed in writing that it wasn’t moving forward with a $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund to compensate Trump allies who believe they were prosecuted for political purposes. Trump demanded the fund as part of a settlement to his lawsuit against the IRS.
RELATED: Blanche drops 'anti-weaponization' fund after GOP senators threaten AG bid
The other side:
Democrats say Blanche’s order doesn’t go far enough to prevent the Trump administration from reviving the fund after the acting attorney general’s confirmation and have called for legislation to permanently bar it.
The order also doesn’t stop the administration from compensating Trump allies — including people who attacked the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — through a previously established process that allows people to file claims for damages if they believed they were wronged by the government.
RELATED: Trump says he'll restore Anti-Weaponization Fund if GOP holdouts reject Blanche
The fund "can easily be revived with a new order from the Department of Justice 15 minutes after Mr. Blanche is confirmed as attorney general," said Dick Durbin of Illinois, the top Democrat on the committee.
Who is Todd Blanche?
The backstory:
Blanche, a former federal prosecutor and key member of Trump’s defense team as he faced four indictments, arrived at the Justice Department last year as deputy attorney general. He was elevated to acting attorney general after Trump fired Bondi.
While Blanche insisted he wasn’t auditioning for the permanent post, he moved swiftly to accelerate investigations into Trump foes and indict former FBI Director James Comey, drawing condemnation from critics who say he has not shed his title as Trump’s personal lawyer.
